passages.text: For example, the leaders among your Egyptians—those who boasted about celestial phenomena and professed to distinguish the natures of the stars—because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them, subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power. For some of them handed down the worship of an ox called Apis, others of a male goat, others of a cat, others of a serpent, and even of a fish, onions, winds from bellies, sewers, and limbs of irrational animals, along with countless other utterly shameful absurdities.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For example
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the phrase introduces the Egyptians as an immediate illustrative case rather than asserting that their conduct occurred at once; a temporal rendering such as “immediately, then” is also lexically possible in other contexts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the leaders among your Egyptians
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχηγέται can denote leaders, originators, or founders. “Leaders” preserves their authoritative role without deciding whether they were regarded specifically as historical founders.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who boasted about celestial phenomena
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ancient μετεωρολογία concerns phenomena aloft, including celestial and atmospheric matters; modern “meteorology” would be too narrow.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts something dwelling or lurking in the innermost recesses, while ὑπό expresses cause or agency.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάσῃ αὐτὸ ἀτιμίᾳ ὅσον τὸ κατ’ αὐτοὺς ὑπέβαλαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter αὐτό has no explicit antecedent within this supplied section, so the translation retains the unresolved pronoun rather than identifying its referent conjecturally.

lexical_decisions.chosen: others of a male goat
lexical_decisions.rationale: τράγος specifically denotes a male goat; the elliptical English continues “handed down the worship” from the preceding clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: winds from bellies, sewers
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεύματα preserves the bodily-wind image, while ὀχετοί denotes drains or sewers in this deliberately degrading list.

passages.text: When Peter had said these things, the crowd standing there laughed. In response to their laughter Peter said, “You laugh at their practices, not knowing that you yourselves are being laughed at far more by them. Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom. I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians, since, although they are rational beings, they worship irrational animals—things certain to die. But hear how those people in turn speak while ridiculing you: ‘Although we worship things that die,’ they say, ‘they at least were once alive, whereas you venerate things that have never been alive.’ In addition, they say, ‘Wanting to honor the form of the one God, and not discovering what it is like, we chose to honor every form.’ Similarly, by saying certain things of this sort, they suppose that their thinking is sounder than yours.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: You laugh at their practices
lexical_decisions.rationale: Γελᾶτε can be indicative or imperative. The accompanying participle “not knowing” supports describing the audience’s conduct, though “Laugh at their practices” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν τὰ ἀλλήλων γελᾶτε· τὰ γὰρ ἴδια ὑπὸ συνηθείας κακῆς εἰς ἀπάτην ἀχθέντες οὐ βλέπετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explanatory γάρ connects their reciprocal ridicule with their failure to perceive their own practices; the participial phrase identifies evil custom as what led them into deception.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι δὲ ὄντως ὀρθῶς καταγελᾶτε τῶν Αἰγυπτίων, σύνφημι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Do indeed” preserves the explicit emphasis of ὄντως, “rightly” renders ὀρθῶς, and “I agree” represents σύνφημι.

lexical_decisions.chosen: ‘Although we ...,’ they say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular parenthetical φησίν functions as a quotation formula within a response introduced as what the Egyptians say, even though the quoted speakers use the plural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to honor every form
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although προτιμάω can mean “prefer” or “honor especially,” “honor” fits the claim that every form was selected as an object of reverence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Similarly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed ὁμῶς is the adverb “alike” or “similarly,” not the more familiar ὅμως, “nevertheless.”

passages.text: “Therefore you too should answer them: ‘You are lying, for it is not out of honor directed toward the God who truly is that you venerate these things. For then all of you would be worshiping every form, which is not what you have been doing. Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war; and similarly all of you, having singled out one thing for honor, fault the objects of others. With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another.’ Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason and ashamed of the manifest disgrace, attempt to turn these things into allegories, wishing through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception. Nevertheless, we would have refuted the allegories as well, had we been there—the allegories of those whom so foolish a passion has mastered as to produce the greatest sickness in their imagination. For the plaster must not be applied to the healthy part of the body, but to the part that is suffering. Since, then, by laughing at the Egyptians’ practices you showed that you had not suffered what they suffer, it was reasonable, regarding the condition from which you yourselves suffer, for me, being here, to provide you with a cure for the condition within you.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τιμῇ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ὄντως θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of honor directed toward the God who truly is
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes honor oriented toward the genuinely existing God; “the true God” is possible but would make the existential wording less visible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which is not what you have been doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἐποιεῖτε points to their established conduct, which contradicts their claim to honor every form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ μὲν γὰρ ὑμῶν κρόμμυον ὑπονοήσαντες εἶναι τὸ θεῖον καὶ γαστρὸς πνεύματα σέβοντες πολεμοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes both participles as describing the shared subject introduced by οἱ μὲν. A material alternative distributes them between rival groups: “Some among you—the ones supposing the divine to be an onion and the ones venerating winds from a belly—wage war.” The ensuing account of each group preferring one object supports that distributive possibility. The Greek does not state an object for “wage war,” so none is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having supposed the divine to be an onion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents τὸ θεῖον as the subject of the infinitive and κρόμμυον as its predicate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having singled out one thing for honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both selection or preference and the religious honor implied by προτιμάω.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διαφόρῳ δὲ γνώμῃ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζῴου μελῶν ὃς μὲν ἄλλο σέβει, ἕτερος δὲ τὸ ἕτερον
lexical_decisions.chosen: With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive μελῶν is represented partitively through “one limb ... another,” while διαφόρῳ γνώμῃ marks the worshipers’ differing judgments.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν αὐτῶν ἔτι τὰ τοῦ ὀρθοῦ λογισμοῦ πνέοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The partitive αὐτῶν is understood with an omitted “some,” while πνέοντες retains the metaphor of breathing or exuding what belongs to sound reasoning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι’ ἑτέρας ἀτονοίας τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης αὐτῶν θανάσιμα κρατύνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀτονία denotes weakness or lack of strength, while the substantival τὰ ... θανάσιμα refers generally to the deadly features or effects belonging to their deception.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὧν τὸ τοσοῦτον μωρὸν ἐπεκράτησεν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: those whom so foolish a passion has mastered
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὧν is taken as the genitive object of ἐπεκράτησεν. It could alternatively be possessive—“whose exceedingly foolish passion became strong enough”—without materially changing the accusation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the plaster
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression supplies the image of a medicinal plaster being applied specifically to the diseased part.

source_issues.issue: The selected print places a high stop between the preposition πρὸς and its object αὐτούς. The syntax requires the words to be construed together; this is treated provisionally as an editorial punctuation anomaly, not as missing wording.

The selected print has the unassimilated compound spelling ἐνποιῆσαι, where the normalized assimilated spelling ἐμποιῆσαι is common. The printed form remains intelligible and has not been silently normalized.

passages.text: The one who chooses to worship God ought first of all to know what alone is distinctive of God’s nature, something that cannot belong to another, so that, by looking to his distinctive property and not finding it in anyone else, he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God. God’s distinctive property is that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all. With respect to power, what makes is greater than what is made; with respect to magnitude, the infinite is greater than the finite; with respect to form, what is most beautiful; with respect to blessedness, what is most blessed; and with respect to intellect, what is most perfect. Likewise, in all other respects he himself possesses superiority beyond comparison. Since, then, as I said, it is distinctive of God that he is superior to all things, and since the world that contains everything has come into being through him, it is absolutely necessary to say that nothing that has come into being through him can stand in equal comparison with him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί μόνον τῆς θεοῦ φύσεως ἴδιόν ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what alone is distinctive of God’s nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον denotes a uniquely proper or distinguishing characteristic, not merely a common attribute.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρῳ τὸ θεῷ εἶναι μὴ ἀπατηθῇ δοῦναί ποτε
lexical_decisions.chosen: he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive phrase literally concerns giving “being God” to another; “status” makes the construction intelligible without reducing it to a divine quality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον μόνον εἶναι, ὡς πάντων ποιητήν, οὕτως καὶ κρείττονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττονα is the predicate of the infinitive, while πάντων explicitly accompanies “maker” and is contextually carried into the comparison. A more structurally literal alternative is “that he alone is, just as maker of all, so also superior.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what makes is greater than what is made
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῦ ποιητοῦ is read as the substantivized verbal adjective ποιητός, “made,” rather than the identically formed genitive of ποιητής, “maker,” since the resulting maker-made contrast fits the argument and the parallel comparisons.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with respect to form, what is most beautiful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative idea “is greater” is carried forward elliptically from κρείττόν ἐστιν, while the Greek supplies no explicit second term for this comparison.

lexical_decisions.chosen: stand in equal comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression denies that anything created can bear a comparison that places it on equal terms with God.

passages.text: But if one who does not possess incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side cannot himself be God, and if the whole world cannot be this insofar as it has come into being, would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God? By “parts” I mean those you call gods, made from gold and silver, bronze and stone, or indeed from any other material whatsoever—and these fashioned by a mortal hand. Nevertheless, in answer to these points, let us see what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἀπαράβλητον καὶ ἀνυπέρβλητον καὶ πάντῃ πάντοθεν ἀνενδεὲς
lexical_decisions.chosen: incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjectives name qualities required of God; πάντῃ πάντοθεν emphatically expresses completeness from every direction or standpoint.

lexical_decisions.chosen: cannot himself be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate “God” is supplied from the surrounding argument and is stated explicitly later in the same sentence; “cannot himself be” would be unintelligibly incomplete in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: insofar as it has come into being
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθό gives the respect or ground on which the world fails the stated criterion: it is something generated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον τὰ μόρια αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως κληθείη θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes οὐκ as framing a rhetorical negative question and ἀλόγως as characterizing the act of calling the parts God. The sequence οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως can alternatively be parsed as “would not unreasonably,” but that reading would reverse the argument developed in the surrounding sentences. The neuter plural subject can take the singular verb κληθείη in Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ταῦτα ὑπὸ θνητῆς χειρὸς δεδημιουργημένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: and these fashioned by a mortal hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα adds emphatic indignation: the alleged gods are not merely material but are manufactured by mortal agency.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷα δι’ ἀνθρώπου στόματος ὁ δεινὸς ὄφις φαρμάσσει τοῖς συριγμοῖς τοὺς ἐξαπατωμένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: φαρμάσσω can mean to drug, poison, or bewitch. “Administers poison” preserves the serpent’s venom image and the instrumental hissings; a less imagistic alternative is “how the terrible serpent drugs or bewitches those who are being deceived.”
